title: DHS Expands $4,000 H-1B and $4,500 L-1 Fees to Cover Same-Employer Extensions
excerpt: A final rule taking effect September 9 adds the 9/11 biometric screening fee to extension petitions, hitting large IT staffing firms and Indian professionals hardest.
body:
• A DHS final rule, effective September 9, extends the $4,000 H-1B and $4,500 L-1 biometric screening fee to same-employer extension petitions — not just initial filings and employer changes.
  • The rule targets employers with 50 or more U.S. employees where at least half the workforce holds H-1B or L-1 status, predominantly large IT staffing and outsourcing firms.
  • DHS estimates the change will generate an additional $37.9 million in FY2026 and $40 million in FY2027 for the biometric entry-exit programme.
  • Indian professionals are disproportionately affected: USCIS data show 72% of H-1B approvals are for continuing employment, with Indians accounting for 77.6% of those renewals.

The Department of Homeland Security has finalised a rule that extends the 9/11 biometric screening fee to H-1B and L-1 visa extension petitions filed by the same employer — a significant expansion of costs for companies that rely heavily on foreign workers.

The final rule, published in the Federal Register and taking effect on September 9, adds a $4,000 fee to H-1B extension-of-stay applications and a $4,500 fee to L-1 intracompany transfer extensions. Previously, these fees applied only when an employer filed an initial petition or when a worker changed employers.

Who Pays and How Much

The rule applies to "covered employers" — businesses with 50 or more U.S.-based employees where at least 50% of the workforce holds H-1B or L-1 status. In practice, this means large IT services and staffing companies, many of them India-headquartered outsourcing firms such as Infosys, TCS and Wipro, along with their U.S.-based counterparts.

https://x.com/iamrakeshbansal/status/2086997014462828807

Under the previous interpretation, the 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee applied to roughly 29% of petitions filed by covered employers. DHS estimates the expanded rule will cover approximately 89% of those filings, according to Bloomberg Law.

The agency projects the change will increase fee collections by $37.9 million in fiscal year 2026 and $40 million in fiscal year 2027. Revenue supports the biometric entry-exit tracking system, which DHS says has identified nearly 2,000 imposters and more than 300,000 visa overstays since 2018.

"These overdue adjustments in fees are necessary to efficiently and fairly administer our nation's lawful immigration system, secure the homeland and protect Americans."

— Joseph Edlow, USCIS Acting Deputy Director for Policy

Stacking Costs Under the Trump Administration

The fee expansion is the latest in a series of cost increases targeting H-1B employers. Last year, a White House proclamation imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B workers hired from outside the United States, leading to a steep decline in new sponsorships. A separate Department of Labor proposal to raise prevailing wage floors for H-1B positions could cost employers as much as $18 billion in its first year, according to Bloomberg Law estimates.

Taken together, the layered fees make extending an H-1B worker's stay substantially more expensive than it was two years ago, particularly for companies that employ large numbers of visa holders.

Disproportionate Impact on Indian Workers

The rule's impact falls disproportionately on Indian nationals. USCIS data show that approximately 72% of H-1B approvals in fiscal year 2025 were for continuing employment — meaning extensions rather than new hires. Indians accounted for about 77.6% of those renewal approvals.

For covered employers extending dozens or hundreds of H-1B workers annually, the cumulative cost increase runs into the millions. Companies may respond by reducing extension filings, relocating work offshore, or absorbing the additional expense — each option carrying its own implications for workers and business operations.

Legal Challenges Likely

The American Immigration Lawyers Association opposed the fee expansion during the public comment period, arguing it contradicts the "plain language and intent" of the underlying statute. AILA noted that a similar attempt to impose these fees on extensions during the first Trump administration was blocked by a nationwide injunction.

Congress first established a supplemental fee on H-1B and L-1 petitions in 2010, then doubled the amount in 2015 when it created the 9/11 Biometric Fee under Public Law 114-113. The fee was originally set to expire on September 30, 2025, but has been extended through September 30, 2027.

What's Next

With the rule taking effect September 9, covered employers have less than a month to adjust their filing strategies and budgets. Immigration attorneys expect legal challenges, citing the same procedural flaws that led to the earlier injunction. For the estimated 600,000-plus H-1B workers in the United States — the majority of them Indian nationals — the rule represents another layer of uncertainty in an increasingly costly and restrictive visa landscape.
